vignette:
Mrs. Rodríguez, seventy-eight years old, sits in the armchair across from me with her back perfectly straight, her small hands folded in her lap. She arrives early for every session, always wearing a neatly pressed blouse, and always apologizes for taking up my time. She worked for thirty-seven years as a call center agent for a major telecommunications company, and even now, in retirement, she keeps a small notepad in her purse to jot down reminders. She tells me she likes to stay organized. It helps her feel in control.

The event that changed everything happened on a Tuesday morning in March of 2019, while she was on her way to work. She was waiting for the bus at her usual stop near the Plaza de la Constitución when a bomb hidden in a trash can detonated less than fifty feet away. She remembers the sound less as a noise and more as a physical force that lifted her off the ground and threw her against a metal railing. She remembers the silence that followed, a thick, ringing silence that seemed to last for minutes before the screaming began. She remembers the smell of burnt metal and something sweet, like caramel, that she later learned was melted plastic from the bus shelter. She was not physically injured—just a few cuts from flying glass—but she has never been the same.

In the weeks and months that followed, Mrs. Rodríguez stopped taking the bus. She walks everywhere now, even if it takes her an hour and a half to get to the grocery store. She avoids the Plaza de la Constitución entirely, taking long detours through residential streets. She tells me she cannot stand crowds, especially groups of people waiting in lines or standing close together. Last month, her daughter invited her to a family birthday party at a restaurant, and Mrs. Rodríguez left after ten minutes because the noise of overlapping conversations made her chest tighten and her vision blur. She stood outside in the parking lot for forty minutes, counting the cars that passed, until she felt calm enough to walk home.

Her sleep is fragmented. She wakes up at 2:47 AM almost every night, the exact time she looked at her watch after the blast. Sometimes she dreams of the sound, but more often she dreams of the silence, of standing alone in a vast empty plaza with no one around, and then the ground begins to shake. She has started sleeping with the television on, tuned to a nature channel, because the sound of human voices makes her feel watched.

At work, before she retired, her colleagues noticed changes. She used to be the warmest voice on the phone, known for her patience with angry customers. But after the bombing, she began to startle at sudden noises—a dropped headset, a slammed door—and would sometimes freeze mid-sentence, staring at the cubicle wall. Her supervisor moved her to a quieter corner, away from the break room, but Mrs. Rodríguez says she could still feel the vibration of footsteps through the floor. She retired early, at sixty-seven, because she could no longer tolerate the unpredictability of other people.

She tells me she feels like a stranger in her own body. She used to love cooking, especially the elaborate holiday meals she learned from her mother in Guadalajara. Now she eats the same thing every day: a bowl of instant oatmeal, a banana, and a cup of tea. She says she cannot concentrate long enough to follow a recipe. She cannot read books anymore, either—the words slide off the page, and she finds herself rereading the same paragraph ten times. She spends most of her days sitting by the window, watching the street, waiting for nothing.

Her husband, who died of a heart attack in 2014, used to tell her she was the bravest person he knew. She thinks about that sometimes, and it makes her sad, because she does not feel brave. She feels small and watchful, like a rabbit that has learned to freeze at the slightest sound. She carries the memory of that Tuesday morning with her everywhere, a weight she cannot set down, a noise that never fully fades.
